newsitem.title: UK: Up to 800,000 refugees at risk in Zaire - Britain.
newsitem.headline: Up to 800,000 refugees at risk in Zaire - Britain.

text.p: Up to 800,000 refugees are at risk in eastern Zaire but they have so far escaped a major outbreak of disease, British aid officials said on Tuesday.
Despite the unexpected return home of 500,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees last weekend, Britain has said it is still committed to sending troops to help with the humanitarian crisis.
On returning from Zaire, a British reconnaissance team briefed military chiefs on Tuesday on how troops could best be deployed.

"It is premature for the international community to conclude that there's nothing to be done because there are hundreds of thousands of refugees unaccounted for," Defence Minister Michael Portillo said.
"We should assume that they will have been penetrated by the armed militia who may be restraining them from returning home," he told the London Times.
Concern is now centred on the fate of refugees in Zaire's Bukavu region with the U.N. refugee agency urging western powers not to abandon plans to send in a military force.
"From 500,000 to 800,000 are at risk," said one British aid official, giving the latest update on the refugee crisis.
"The trouble is that, until we have access to them, it is impossible to say what the potential role of troops could be," the senior official said.
But the Rwanda government insisted there were hardly any refugees left in the region and there was no longer any need for the planned Canadian-led multinational peace force.

Hailing the mass return to Rwanda at the weekend, British officials said those refugees were in relatively good condition and were now dispersing to their communes. "That problem is dealable with," one official said.
Uncertainty surrounded the fate of hundreds of thusands of refugees in the Bukavu region but at least there were no confirmed reports yet of any dysentery or cholera outbreaks, officials said.
Washington has tentatively decided not to send troops to Zaire but will instead use U.S. military cargo planes to fly humanitarian aid to Rwanda, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.
Countries who said they would join the force are to meet on Thursday at the U.S. military's European headquarters in Stuttgart, Germany, to review the situation.
Portillo said he envisaged Britain sending 1,000 "frontline" troops with additional support units. They would be protected by an artillery battery. They are now on 72-hour standby.
"The number one priority for me is to make sure our forces are properly protected," he said.

"It's better to carry a proper deterrent and avoid the risk that someone will take you on than to go too lightly armed and risk an aggressor thinking that he can get the better of our forces," he added.
